title: Noah's cedars (Tanchuma Noach 5)
hookLine: Noah planted and cut cedars for years so people would ask why, and turn
tomorrow: a palace in flames, nobody in sight. who's in charge?

cards: Some things get a question every time: a tattoo, a bracelet you never take off, a mezuzah on a doorpost. People ask, what's that? Midrash Tanchuma imagines Noah doing that on purpose.
Before the flood, it says, he didn't just build. He planted cedar trees, and then he cut them down.

teach.b: People kept walking by. What are these cedars for? And Noah answered: the Master of the world is bringing a flood, and told me to make an ark.
In the midrash, the question was the point.
Every cedar was an invitation to ask, and every answer was a chance to turn.
They mocked him instead. That changes the story. In this telling the flood isn't an ambush.
There was time, and a man in the open with saws and seedlings, answering anyone who asked. Noah kept planting anyway. They could have asked, and listened.
Now the week, back as one picture. A plan drawn before the building. A world chosen, not perfect.
An urge that builds houses. A garden on loan. One family.
And a builder whose slow work was a question left open for his neighbors.

how: Midrash Tanchuma is read alongside the weekly Torah portion; this passage belongs to Noach, the portion of the flood, read in synagogues in the fall.

o: trees Noah grew and cut so people would ask why
a forest the flood washed away before the rain stopped
the wood God told Noah to use for the ark's roof

games.q: the cedars, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: planted and cut in the open
a flood is coming; I'm making an ark

s: in the midrash, the flood came with no warning
Noah's cedars were a long, public warning, and anyone could ask.
Noah planted the very trees he later cut
so people would ask what they were for.

games.q: a classmate notices the mezuzah on your door and asks what it is. you're shy about faith stuff. by Noah's cedars, what's the move?
o: answer plainly and warmly; the asking is the point.
change the subject; faith should stay out of sight.
give a long speech so they never have to ask again.
games.why: in Tanchuma the cedars were there to be asked about, and the answer was the chance.

practice: Choose one thing you do that someone might ask about: a blessing before food, a candle on Friday night, a habit you keep. In one or two sentences, say out loud how you'd answer if a stranger asked why.
Keep it plain and warm, then sit with the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Noah's cedars: in Midrash Tanchuma, trees planted and cut in the open, so people would ask why and have the chance to turn.

orig.note: Hebrew: cedars, the trees Noah plants and cuts in Midrash Tanchuma.

carryVoice: For the road: they could have asked, and the cedars kept the question open. Day fifteen seventy-five, a week built.

sources.ref: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 5 (Noah plants and cuts cedars; people ask, he warns of the flood, they mock)
Genesis 6:13–22 (God tells Noah to make an ark)
